title: Movement & Fitness
description: Movement, play and fitness: fundamental movement skills, balance and coordination, yoga, games and teamwork, components of fitness, traditional Indian games and sports, training principles and lifelong active living. Every lesson is mostly doing, not watching.

objectives: Perform basic movements: run, jump, hop, crawl

explanation: Our bodies can move in so many ways! We can run, jump, hop on one foot, skip, crawl and roll.
We can move fast like a cheetah or slow like a tortoise, big like an elephant or small like a mouse.
Moving every day makes our muscles and bones strong, our heart healthy, and it's fun! Children should be active for at least an hour a day.

explanation: Balancing means keeping steady without falling. Try standing on one leg like a flamingo! Spreading your arms out and looking at one spot helps.

To throw, step forward with the opposite foot to your throwing hand and swing your arm. Practise makes it easier every time.

lessons.title: Strong and Calm Like a Tree
objectives: Hold simple yoga poses safely
Use slow breathing to feel calm
explanation: Yoga combines poses (asanas), breathing and calm attention. It comes from India and is practised around the world.
Many poses are named after nature: tree pose (vrikshasana), cobra pose (bhujangasana), butterfly pose and cat–cow. They make our bodies strong and flexible.
Slow, deep breaths through the nose help our bodies and minds feel calm. Never force a pose — yoga should never hurt.

context.text: Yoga has roots in ancient Indian traditions, with philosophical texts such as the Yoga Sutras of Patanjali. Modern posture-based yoga developed further in the 20th century. International Day of Yoga is observed on 21 June.

vocabulary.meaning: practice of poses, breathing and attention from India

examples: Tree pose: stand on one leg, foot on the other leg's calf or thigh, hands together.
Butterfly pose: sit with soles of feet together and gently flap knees.

lessons.title: Playing Fair
objectives: Follow rules in simple games

explanation: Games have rules so they are fair and fun for everyone. Rules tell us how to play, how to score and what is not allowed.
Good players take turns, play safely, and are kind. Winning is fun, and losing is part of the game too — shake hands and say "good game".

lessons.title: Kho-Kho and Kabaddi
objectives: Explain the basic rules of kho-kho and kabaddi
Play a traditional game safely as a team
explanation: Kho-kho is a chasing game. Chasers sit in a row facing alternate directions; one chaser runs, and can tag a teammate by touching their back and saying "kho" to let them take over the chase.

Kabaddi is a contact team sport. A raider enters the opponents' half and tries to tag defenders and return, all while chanting "kabaddi, kabaddi" on a single breath. Defenders try to stop them. It is now played professionally and internationally.
Other traditional games include lagori (knocking down a stack of stones and rebuilding it), gilli-danda and stapu (hopscotch). They need little equipment and build speed, agility and teamwork.

vocabulary.meaning: a chasing team game from India
a contact team sport where raiders chant on one breath

examples: Lagori needs only a ball and a stack of flat stones.

lessons.title: Exercise Superpowers
objectives: Explain several benefits of exercise for body and mind
Plan a balanced active day
explanation: Exercise strengthens the heart and lungs, so they work better. Activities like running, skipping and jumping make bones stronger.
Exercise also helps the mind: it can improve mood, reduce stress, help us sleep better and even help us concentrate in class.
Health guidelines suggest children aged 5–17 get at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity daily, and limit long periods of sitting and recreational screen time.

context.text: World Health Organization guidelines recommend an average of 60 minutes per day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity for children and adolescents aged 5–17.

lessons.title: Testing My Fitness
objectives: Name the main components of fitness
Conduct simple fitness tests and set goals
explanation: Fitness has several components. Stamina (endurance) is keeping going for a long time. Strength is how much force muscles produce. Speed is moving quickly. Flexibility is how far joints can move.
Skill-related components include balance, coordination (moving body parts together smoothly) and agility (changing direction quickly).

Simple tests measure these: shuttle runs (agility/speed), sit-and-reach (flexibility), standing broad jump (power), and timed skipping or jogging (stamina). Compare yourself with your own past results, not others.

vocabulary.meaning: the ability to keep going for a long time

examples: A marathon runner needs stamina.
A gymnast needs flexibility and balance.

lessons.title: How Skills Improve
objectives: Explain how deliberate practice improves skills
Describe teamwork and communication in sport
explanation: Skills improve through deliberate practice: focused repetition of a specific skill with feedback, slightly beyond what feels easy. Breaking a skill into parts helps.
In team sports, players communicate (calling for the ball, encouraging), take roles, and support each other. A team of good communicators often beats a team of brilliant individuals.
Indian athletes show what practice can achieve: P. V. Sindhu (badminton), Neeraj Chopra (javelin, Olympic gold 2020 Tokyo Games), Mary Kom (boxing) and the hockey teams of the past and present.

context.text: Neeraj Chopra won the men's javelin gold at the Tokyo Olympic Games held in 2021 (officially "Tokyo 2020"); P. V. Sindhu won Olympic medals in 2016 and 2021.

lessons.title: The FITT Principle
objectives: Explain FITT and progressive overload
Design a safe personal training plan
explanation: FITT guides training: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long) and Type (what activity).
Progressive overload means gradually increasing demands so the body adapts — a little more distance, time or repetitions each week. Increasing too fast risks injury.
Rest and recovery are part of training: muscles adapt and repair during rest, especially sleep. Specificity means training matches your goal — swimmers swim, runners run.

vocabulary.meaning: rest that allows the body to repair and adapt

examples: Running 2 km three times a week, adding a little each week.
Rest days between hard sessions.

story.title: Too Much, Too Soon
story.text: Ravi decided to get fit and ran 10 km on his first day. The next morning he could barely walk and missed a week. His PE teacher helped him plan: 2 km three times a week, adding 10% each week. Two months later, Ravi ran 5 km happily — and injury-free.

lessons.title: RICE and Injury Prevention
objectives: Describe ways to prevent sports injuries
Apply basic first aid for minor sprains and know when to seek medical help
prerequisites: Knows warm-ups and first aid basics
explanation: Prevention: warm up, use correct technique, wear suitable shoes and protective gear, build up gradually, stay hydrated, and rest when tired. In Indian summers, avoid intense exercise in the hottest hours.

A sprain is an injury to a ligament (joint), like a twisted ankle; a strain is an injury to a muscle. For minor sprains and strains, a common first-aid approach is RICE: Rest, Ice (wrapped, not directly on skin, for short periods), Compression (a bandage), Elevation (raise it).
See a doctor for severe pain, swelling, inability to bear weight, a possible broken bone, or a head injury. Never play on after a head injury — stop and get checked.

vocabulary.meaning: injury to a ligament at a joint
a brain injury from a blow to the head

examples: Wearing shin guards in football.
Drinking water before, during and after sport in the heat.

story.title: Sitting Out
story.text: In the final minutes of a match, Asha bumped heads with another player and felt dizzy. She wanted to keep playing, but her coach insisted she sit out and see a doctor. "Your brain is more important than any match," the coach said. Asha recovered fully and was back the following month.

lessons.title: Aerobic and Anaerobic Exercise
objectives: Explain aerobic and anaerobic respiration in exercise
Use heart rate to monitor intensity
prerequisites: Understands respiration and the circulatory system
explanation: In aerobic respiration, muscles use oxygen to release energy from glucose: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water (+ energy). It powers steady, longer activity like jogging.

In intense bursts, muscles can't get enough oxygen, so they also use anaerobic respiration: glucose → lactic acid (+ less energy). This powers sprints but can't last long. Afterwards, you breathe hard to repay the "oxygen debt".

Training causes adaptations: a stronger heart pumping more blood per beat (lower resting heart rate), more capillaries, and more efficient muscles. Heart rate zones help gauge intensity; a rough estimate of maximum heart rate is 220 minus age.

vocabulary.meaning: a product of anaerobic respiration in muscles
extra oxygen needed after intense exercise

examples: Marathon running is mainly aerobic.
A 100 m sprint relies heavily on anaerobic energy.

story.title: The Burning Legs
story.text: In the last 50 metres of a 400 m race, Kabir's legs burned and felt heavy. His coach explained afterwards: "Your muscles switched to anaerobic energy. It's fast but tiring. Training will make your aerobic system stronger so you can hold your speed longer."

lessons.title: Sport, Fairness and Society
objectives: Analyse issues of equality, ethics and inclusion in sport
Design a lifelong physical activity plan
explanation: Sport reflects society. Access to sport has often been unequal by gender, income, caste, region and disability. Initiatives like Khelo India aim to widen participation.
Ethics in sport includes fair play, anti-doping rules (which protect health and fairness), and respect for opponents and officials.

Para-sport showcases elite athletes with disabilities; India's para-athletes, such as Avani Lekhara (shooting) and Sumit Antil (javelin), have won Paralympic gold. For most people, the goal is lifelong activity — finding enjoyable movement that continues for decades.

context.text: At the Tokyo Paralympic Games (held in 2021), Avani Lekhara won gold in shooting and Sumit Antil won gold in javelin (F64).

vocabulary.meaning: using banned substances to enhance performance

examples: Women's cricket and hockey gaining wider audiences.
